doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Church, the blues and the devil's music
summary: Asked about faith versus jazz, he recalls church sermons, being baptized as a boy, and hearing blues-based music.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Was there ever a conflict between your choice of jazz oriented music and your spirituality? Was there any kind of — these don’t work together for you?

Well as a kid I’d heard that the blues and rhythm was the devil’s music. And I didn’t really listen to the blues that much. I heard it, because it was a part of the scene. Getting back to that high school thing, I remember hearing Louis Jordan swing on the jukebox, singing “Caldonia” and all those things, and I’d see them in movies and I heard Tommy Dorsey’s [scats] and he’d play that long trombone solo on it, which was very nice. And I loved those things. They were all based on the blues. And of course the church was in there too, I used to go to church all the time and I’d hear them sing. And I knew that there was a difference between the church and the school, it didn’t seem real. It seemed to me like church was unrealistic as compared to what I experienced everyday in school. It seems like some kind of pie in the sky thing. Because he always preached the same sermons and it was always hell and — what do you call it? Hell and brimstone or something.

You know unless you come up and give me your hand and do such a thing, he says, you’re going to die and go to hell in a minute. So and what about that? My buddies, speaking about that hell and brimstone thing, my buddies you know, we were all about nine or ten years old. They were a little bit older than I was. So I saw them go up and get the preacher’s hand one day. And they says well it’s very nice that these young men have joined the church. So I didn’t want to be outdone by my buddies so I went up there and gave the preacher my hand. And he asked me some questions and I turned my head and whispered, the low part of my voice, and he would translate to the audience and, “well that’s very fine.” So we were all baptized and I was with my buddies again. And that’s how that part of it started, that church thing. And that’s all there was to do.
